Mom! Dad! There's a giant yellow arrow floating over our house!
It's 7 a.m. You're standing outside in your pajamas. A huge yellow arrow is spinning above your roof.
And above your own head, in tiny glowing letters, it says: health, one hundred percent.
Why do I have a health bar?!
You run back inside. Dad is holding his coffee. There's a money counter floating above his head.
It says I have three hundred and twelve dollars. That's actually correct. That's terrifying.
The news says the whole world turned into a video game overnight. Like GTA Six.
Does that mean I can drive a car?
So, what happens next? Day one is fun. Day two is weird. And by day thirty... well. Let's see.
Day one. Your neighbor Gary is watering his lawn.
You say hi. He says it again.
He has said that exact sentence four hundred times since sunrise. He looks very tired.
Then Dad drops a gum wrapper on the sidewalk. Ding. A white star appears above his head.
Ding. Two stars. A police car comes around the corner. Siren on. For a gum wrapper.
Pick it up! Pick it up!
Dad picks it up. The stars blink and disappear. The police car drives away like nothing happened.
This is going to be a long month.
Dad gets in the car to go to work. The radio turns on by itself. There is only one station.
Buy the Super Suck Three Thousand! The vacuum that sucks so good, it sucks!
How do I turn this off?
You can't. Every car in the world now plays the same radio. Forever.
Day two. Mom goes to the supermarket. In front of the milk, there's a glowing yellow circle on the floor.
She steps into it. Trumpets play. Big letters appear: mission complete.
Plus fifty respect. Mom now has more respect than the mayor.
Ma'am... can I have your autograph?
Day three. You trip over the garden hose. You fall. Everything turns gray.
One second later, you're standing outside the hospital. Totally fine. Minus one hundred dollars.
Wait. I didn't even get hurt. Why am I paying?
Respawn fee, sweetie. See you tomorrow.
She's right. You trip again the next day. And the day after that.
You now have a loyalty card. Ten respawns, and the eleventh one is free.
Day five. Dad gets two stars for driving three miles over the speed limit. The police follow him everywhere.
Then he sees a garage with a giant spray can on the roof. He drives in. The door closes.
The door opens. The car is bright purple. The stars are gone. The police drive right past him.
They don't recognize me! I'm a genius!
You're driving a purple car, honey. Everybody recognizes you.
Dad does it again the next day. And the next. The car is now orange. Then green. Then gold.
Day seven. Your sister finds out about cheat codes.
She presses it on the TV remote. Outside, it starts raining. Rubber ducks.
It rains rubber ducks for three hours. The whole street is yellow and squeaky.
Nobody laughs. Okay, you laugh a little.
Give me that remote. Right now.
Day nine. Dad goes to work. Everyone in the office walks in little circles. Nobody actually works.
Then a yellow arrow appears above his boss's head.
I've got a job for you. Deliver this pizza across town in ninety seconds. If the timer hits zero, you fail.
A giant timer appears in the sky. Ninety. Eighty-nine. Dad runs. He trips. The pizza flies. The timer hits zero.
Huge red letters: mission failed. Dad has to start over.
He tries seventeen times. On the eighteenth try, he makes it with one second left.
I have never been so proud of a pizza.
Day ten. You go to school. Your teacher has a yellow arrow above her head too.
Side mission. Finish this math test in five minutes. Reward: two hundred respect.
You can't skip algebra, sweetie. Nobody can.
You fail. Mission failed. The whole class starts over at question one. You take the same math test eleven times.
By the eleventh try, you know every answer by heart. One hundred percent. Plus two hundred respect.
I hate that this actually worked.
Day twelve. You're on the couch. Dad is reading something on his phone.
Listen to this. In 2013, GTA Five made one billion dollars in just three days. Faster than any movie or game before it.
One billion dollars? In three days?
And now we live inside the next one. For free. Where's my billion?
That part is real, by the way. The company behind the game announced it in 2013.
Day fourteen. The family goes to the beach. Everyone in town is there, doing the exact same thing.
Jogging in a straight line. Turning around. Jogging back. Again and again.
Mom, that man has been jogging for six hours.
Dad rents a jet ski. He crashes into the pier after four seconds. Everything turns gray.
Dad is back outside the hospital. Soaking wet. Minus one hundred dollars.
Day sixteen. Your sister finds a glowing teddy bear in the bushes. A message pops up: hidden teddy, one of one hundred.
One of one hundred? I'm finding all of them.
She searches the garden. The roof. The shed. Gary's dog house.
Day eighteen. Mom now has so much respect, every restaurant gives her free food.
Waiters line up just to bring her bread.
I could get used to this.
Can I have some bread too?
Sorry, sir. Your respect level is too low.
I delivered a pizza eighteen times!
Day nineteen. Dad wants a new car. He counts all his money.
Three hundred and twelve dollars. Minus four hospital visits. Minus seven paint jobs. He has eleven dollars left.
What can I get for eleven dollars?
A bicycle. Pink. With a little bell.
It's fine. Nobody chases a pink bicycle.
Ding. One star. He forgot to ring the bell.
Day twenty-one. Things get weird. Nobody waits at red lights anymore. Everybody gets stars. Everybody gets chased.
There are now more police cars than normal cars. They are mostly chasing each other. Nobody remembers why.
Says the guy with a loyalty card at the hospital.
Day twenty-four. Mom has an idea.
If this is a game, there has to be a save button somewhere.
The family searches the whole house. Under the couch. Inside the fridge. Even in Dad's car.
Super Suck Three Thousand! It sucks so good!
Then you find it. A glowing floppy disk, floating right above your bed.
Guys! When I sleep in my bed, the game saves!
So if something goes wrong, we just load?
Day twenty-six. You get an idea. What if everybody does the missions together?
Gary carries the pizzas. Mom stops the traffic with pure respect. Your sister holds the timer.
The whole street does Dad's pizza mission in twelve seconds. Mission complete. Plus one thousand respect. For everyone.
Turns out, even in a video game, nobody wins alone.
Day thirty. You wake up. The arrow is gone. The health bar is gone. The map in the sky is gone.
You run downstairs. Mom is normal. Dad is normal. Even the radio is quiet.
No stars. No money counter. Just me and my coffee. Beautiful.
Then the TV turns on by itself. Big letters fill the screen. Update downloading: zombie mode.
Outside the window, Gary is standing on the lawn. Very still. Very green.
